q: Why did the internet fight a decade over .xxx domains?

brew.q: Why did the internet fight a decade over .xxx domains?

titles: The Internet Fought 10 Years Over 3 Letters
Porn and Conservatives Agreed on One Thing

beats.vo: The internet's rulebook spent ten years arguing about three letters.
beats.visual: Paper diorama world. A giant cardboard boardroom table stretches into fog. Three cut-out letters, X X X, sit in the center under a spotlight. At the head of the table, the penguin in a tiny paper judge's robe slowly lowers its glasses.

beats.vo: In 2000, a company asked ICANN, the group that approves domain endings, for a new one: dot x x x.
beats.visual: A paper envelope slides across the table. Behind the penguin, a wall of approved endings hangs like shop signs: .com, .org, .net. The penguin sniffs the envelope suspiciously.

beats.vo: The pitch was simple. Put adult websites in one labeled neighborhood. Easy to find, easy to filter.
beats.visual: A pop-up paper city unfolds. One street gets a red folded-paper gate stamped XXX. Tiny cardboard buildings shuffle behind it like obedient chess pieces.

beats.vo: ICANN said no. The company came back in 2004. This time, ICANN leaned yes.
beats.visual: The penguin slams a huge rubber stamp: DENIED. Calendar pages flutter like confetti. The envelope returns. The penguin tilts its head, stamp hovering over APPROVED.

beats.vo: Then the letters poured in. Conservative groups said it would make porn look official. Governments raised concerns too.
beats.visual: An avalanche of paper letters buries the table. The penguin climbs out on top, reading one, eyes narrowing, a tiny paper flag of a government seal stuck to its head.

beats.vo: So ICANN flipped, and rejected it again in 2007.
beats.visual: The penguin turns the APPROVED stamp upside down. It now reads DENIED. It stamps the envelope three times, very calmly.

beats.vo: Here's the twist. The adult industry hated it too.
beats.visual: Camera pulls back. On one side, paper picket signs from conservative groups. On the other, velvet-curtained cardboard studios with their own picket signs. Both crowds point at the red gate. The penguin looks back and forth, delighted.

beats.vo: Porn sites feared a digital ghetto. One switch, and governments could block the whole street.
beats.visual: Inside the red-gated street, a single paper lever appears. The penguin pulls it. The whole street folds flat like a closing pop-up book.

beats.vo: The company fought back with an independent review, and in 2010 the panel sided with it.
beats.visual: A three-figure paper tribunal rises from the floor. A gavel drops. The penguin's stamp cracks in half. It pretends nothing happened.

beats.vo: In 2011, it finally launched. Brands and universities paid to lock their names away.
beats.visual: The red gate opens. Paper university crests and corporate logos rush in, each buying a padlock and locking an empty door with its own name on it. The penguin sells the padlocks from a little booth.

beats.vo: Ten years. Three letters. Everyone mad. Sounds like the internet.
beats.visual: Back at the giant table, now empty. The three letters sit under the spotlight. The penguin sweeps them into a drawer, closes it, and the light clicks off.

verify: ICM Registry first applied for .xxx in ICANN's 2000 new TLD round and reapplied in 2004 as a sponsored TLD
ICANN board tentatively approved .xxx in 2005 before pressure from conservative groups and governments, including the US Department of Commerce and ICANN's Government Advisory Committee
ICANN rejected .xxx in 2006 and again in March 2007
An Independent Review Process panel ruled in ICM's favor in February 2010
ICANN approved .xxx in March 2011 and it launched to the public in December 2011
Adult industry opposition, including the Free Speech Coalition, centered on fears of censorship, mandatory segregation, and defensive registration costs
Universities and brands bought defensive blocking registrations during the launch period
